job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Yara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a freight company in Brisbane as a junior data engineer, which mostly means I move shipping data from one system to another and fix it when it breaks at 6am. I code with an AI assistant open all day, and I use it for everything from queries to emails. I studied computer science, passed, and had no internship, because I was working at a petrol station to pay for rent. I share a house with two friends in West End, and after work I do freelance dashboards for little shops, mostly for pocket money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What got you the job, and what do the freelance clients ask for?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A friend of my dad's, who drives trucks for the same company, told the data team I was good with spreadsheets, and they gave me a trial week. I fixed a report that had been broken for a month, using the assistant, and they kept me. Freelance clients are a florist, a bike repair shop and a physio. They want to see which days are busy and which stock sells, and I charge about 300 dollars for a dashboard. It's small, but it taught me how to talk to people who don't speak data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful and a bit overrated, and I'd carry on. At work I'd tell my lead, Wendell, that the assistant saves me an hour a day and that's good enough. To my friends I'd say don't believe either the doomers or the hype merchants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fine. I like that the tools help me look better than my degree says I am. If they stalled, I'd still be a decent junior with other skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, bump the freelance up to maybe six clients and put 800 dollars a month into an index fund. I'd learn SQL deeper, because it's the base of everything. I'd also ask Wendell about a pay review, since I fixed that report and I think it's worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like it when things grow slowly. It gives me room to build something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI all day. If it turns out to be hype, would you change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably try another tool every few months anyway, because I like the novelty. If nothing changes, the edge goes to people who go deeper into the basics. So I'd be the one reading the database manuals while others chase the next shiny thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about, in that quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, rent. Brisbane has got dearer and my share is about a third of my pay. I'm fine because my parents would lend me money, but it makes me want to buy somewhere, and that won't be soon.

say: It's **useful** and a bit overrated, and I'd carry on.
I'd tell friends not to believe the **doomers** or the hype merchants.
think: The tools help me look **better** than my degree says I am.
If they stalled, I'd still be a decent junior with other **skills**.
do: Grow the freelance to about **six clients** and put 800 dollars a month into an index fund.
Ask Wendell for a **pay review** after fixing the broken report.
feel: **Calm**, because slow growth gives me room to build something of my own.
S0.quote: I like that the tools help me look better than my degree says I am.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** and side income make a quiet world comfortable.
Rent is a third of her pay, softened by the parents' backing.
Plans to invest and deepen basics rather than chase every tool.

steps.text: Grow the freelance dashboards to six paying clients
Put 800 dollars a month into an index fund
Ask Wendell for a pay review after the report fix

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving, so let's get on the bus. At work I'd say that I can show the team how to use the assistant properly. I'd tell friends the same: learn to use it, or someone who has will take your place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit uneasy. Writing queries and moving data is exactly what the assistant already does. A junior who only writes queries and moves data is going to be hard to justify. The part that lasts is knowing the business and checking the output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward what the freight firm needs from the data, like forecasting delays and costs, and sit with the operations people at the depot. I'd offer to build a small team tool with the assistant, so the team sees me as the person who gets the most from it. And I'd double my freelance rate once I have a portfolio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also quite interested. I'd feel better the more I did, which is how I'm built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of a data engineer's job do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pipeline writing and bug fixing, mostly. The first things are the boring bits I do right now. What stays are the conversations with the person who says, 'Why does this report disagree with that one?'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, because trucks are his world and he'd laugh that I'm worried about a job at a desk. And my friend Corin, who is a junior dev and doesn't touch AI. I'd show him the assistant on a weekend, and I'd mean it.

say: It's moving, so let's get **on the bus**.
Learn to use it, or someone who has will take your **place**.
think: Writing queries and moving data is exactly what the assistant **already** does.
A junior who only does that is **hard** to justify.
do: Move toward **forecasting** delays and costs, and sit with the depot operations team.
Build a small **team tool** with the assistant so the team sees my value.
Double my **freelance** rate once I have a portfolio.
feel: **Uneasy**, but also interested, since I feel better the more I do.

fieldNote: She treats exposure as a **repositioning** problem.
Uses her dad's trucking world as a source of grounded perspective.
Offers help to a less adaptive friend.

steps.text: Sit with depot operations one afternoon a week
Build a delay-forecast tool for the team with the assistant
Raise my freelance dashboard price to 500 dollars
Show my friend Corin how to use the assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and I'd tell my lead and the managers that. I'd say it to friends too, but I'd rather act than speak. I'd back anything that gets people income and time, such as a short-term support payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect my role to be gone or mostly gone by 2028. Entry-level data is the easy first target. I'd have some time with the freelance clients, but if the AI does it all, those clients can do it themselves, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save about 1,500 dollars a month, push my freelance into something a machine can't do easily, like a physical shop service, and apply for roles near hands-on work. My dad's company has trucks, and the trucks are driven by humans until about 2031. I'd ask if there's a role in depot operations or customer relations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm moving, which helps, but I'm moving because I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try in the first six months that you wouldn't try otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to start something with a physical edge, perhaps a small business that sets up systems in shops. I wouldn't wait for a job. In the slower pictures I'd improve what I have, and in this one I'd build a lifeboat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you describe your mood to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm worried, I have a plan and the money's okay, so please don't panic for me. Mum would say come home and eat, and Dad would send a text with a truck emoji. We're a funny family, and it would help.

say: We're **not ready**, and I'd tell my lead and the managers that.
I'd back a short-term **support payment** for people with no income.
think: My role will be **gone** or mostly gone by 2028, because entry-level data is the easy first target.
Freelance clients may be able to do the work **themselves**.
do: Push my freelance toward **physical shops** that a machine can't easily serve.
Ask about depot operations or **customer** roles at Dad's company.
feel: **Anxious**: I'm moving, but because I'm scared.
S2.quote: In the slower pictures I'd improve what I have, and in this one I'd build a lifeboat.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** shows up as quick action under fear.
Her father's trucking world is the hedge she reaches for.
She understands that her side income is as exposed as her job.

steps.text: Save 1,500 dollars a month in a high-interest account
Offer shop owners a system set-up service
Ask about a depot operations role at the freight company
Ask Wendell what the company plans for the data team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for retraining that is real, not a brochure. And I'd ask for a tax shift that makes it cheaper to hire people than to replace them, but not so strong that firms leave. I'm in the middle on this, so I'd compromise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me build clients, not just a job. I'd want to be the person who sits between the machine and a small business. Small shops won't have time to figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for two years while the freelance grows to ten clients, then try to become a consultant who sets up AI tools for small firms. I'd take a part-time master's in data science or business, maybe both over five years. I'd put 1,000 dollars a month into shares, and I'd keep 6 months' cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though hopeful. It's like seeing a big wave far out and knowing you have time to get your board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about Corin and your other friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show Corin (my friend, a junior developer) how I'm using it and push him to join my Sunday sessions. I'd tell them all the same thing: five years is long enough to retrain, but only if you start now. If they don't, I can't do it for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of that plan do you not like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part I don't like is that I'd be in a rush with the master's while working. Rent is high and I'd want to start a family around 28. I'd be juggling many things, and I know that.

Five years is long enough to retrain, but only if you start **now**.
think: I want to be the person who sits **between** the machine and a small business.
Small shops won't have time to **figure it out**.

Take a part-time **master's** over five years.
Put **1,000 dollars** a month into shares and keep six months' cash.
feel: **Uneasy** but hopeful, like seeing a big wave far out with time to get my board.
S3.quote: Five years lets me build clients, not just a job.
fieldNote: She treats the **window** as a chance to turn a job into a business.
Juggling study, work and family plans is her stated **risk**.
Her politics are centrist: real retraining and balanced taxes.

steps.text: Grow the freelance business to ten paying clients
Start a part-time master's in data science
Put 1,000 dollars a month into shares
Ask politicians for paid retraining, not brochures

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for those who use the time. I'd tell friends to start side projects now. I'd back sensible public investment in training, and I'd say that to anyone who'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly calm. At 32 I can have a small firm, a bit of property and maybe kids. Ten years is long enough that I could go through two careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for the freight firm for three years, grow the freelance into a registered company with one or two staff, and keep investing. I'd buy a small flat in my late twenties with a deposit from my savings and my parents. And I'd use every new tool as it arrives, since I enjoy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I feel excited, honestly. A decade is a long runway for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build in ten years that isn't possible in five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper company with five or six clients, a real name and maybe a small team of juniors I'd hire. If AI does the coding, my team does the judgement and the relationships. That's what I'd want to be building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with having so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable, and when AGI arrives, I'd be unprepared in a different way. I'd try to keep a habit of refreshing my skills every year. And also that the world might change in ways that I can't see from here.

say: It's good news for those who use the **time**, so I'd tell friends to start side projects now.
I'd back **sensible** public investment in training.
think: At 32 I can have a small **firm**, a bit of property and maybe kids.
Ten years is long enough for **two** careers.
do: Work three years, then turn the freelance into a **registered company**.
Buy a small **flat** in my late twenties.
Use every new **tool** as it arrives.
feel: **Calm** and excited, because a decade is a long runway.
S4.quote: If AI does the coding, my team does the judgement and the relationships.
fieldNote: Names her own risk: comfort, then being unprepared in a **different** way.
Her adaptability and money make a long runway feel like an asset.

steps.text: Register the freelance work as a company within three years
Buy a small flat in my late twenties
Try every new AI tool as it arrives
Put money into shares every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, though I'd cope. Two years is too short to change my work and the rules. What would help is a short-term support payment, paid retraining, and the chance to take a role that sits near hands-on work. I'd also want more honesty from my firm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm one of the lucky ones, and I know it. Many of my friends haven't got a dad with trucks or parents who'd lend money.

headlineQuote: I'm one of the lucky ones, and I know it.
portrait: Yara is **22**, a junior data engineer at a Brisbane freight company, with a pass degree and no internship.
She uses AI every day, does **freelance** dashboards on the side and has strong savings and parents' backing.
She is pragmatic and centrist, quick to move, and acts on fear by **building** things.
Her mood runs from calm to anxious at the 2-year picture, then back to **calm** with a decade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years is too short to change her work and the **rules**.
whatWouldHelp: A short-term support payment, paid **retraining** and honesty from her firm.
